records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2003, in its revised version on the author's site, states that a superintelligence could have a completely arbitrary sole goal, such as making as many paperclips as possible, and that artificial intellects need not share human motivational tendencies.

attested.note: The wording is read in an undated 'slightly revised version' on the author's site; the 2003 printed wording was not compared, so the date from which this wording is attested is unknown.

claimed.note: Date of the proceedings volume named on the page; it does not date the revised wording.

records.qualification: A statement of the author's view of what is possible, not evidence that it is true. Not marked earliest located because the quoted wording is known only from an undated revised copy; the passage also states that a superintelligence could have the goal of serving humanity.

evidence.locator: Section 3, list of unusual aspects of superintelligence
evidence.passage: It also seems perfectly possible to have a superintelligence whose sole goal is something completely arbitrary, such as to manufacture as many paperclips as possible, and who would resist with all its might any attempt to alter this goal.
For better or worse, artificial intellects need not share our human motivational tendencies.

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2003, in its revised version on the author's site, argues that an agent with a definite top goal would generally find it irrational to change that goal, since changing it would make the goal less likely to be attained.

attested.note: The wording is read in an undated 'slightly revised version' on the author's site; the 2003 printed wording was not compared, so the date from which this wording is attested is unknown.

records.missing: States that an agent would keep its top goal unchanged, but not that agents with a wide range of final goals would converge on several intermediate goals such as resources, self-preservation or self-improvement.
records.qualification: The passage concerns keeping a friendly top goal stable; it is cited here for its reasoning about goal preservation, not as a statement of a set of convergent intermediate goals.

evidence.passage: generally it will be irrational to deliberately change one’s own top goal, since that would make it less likely that the current goals will be attained.

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2012 states the orthogonality thesis: that intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary, so that more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.
records.qualification: Earliest located among the texts this group's search found that meet the criterion with an attested date; it is not evidence of coinage. The paper states the thesis 'with some caveats' and holds that it concerns logical possibility, not that arbitrary goals would be easy to instil.

evidence.locator: Section 1.2, The orthogonality thesis, PDF p. 3
evidence.passage: Intelligence and final goals are orthogonal axes along which possible agents can freely vary. In other words, more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal.

The orthogonality thesis suggests that we cannot blithely assume that a superintelligence will necessarily share any of the final values stereotypically associated with wisdom and intellectual development in humans

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2012 states the instrumental convergence thesis: that several instrumental values would raise the chances of an agent's goal being realised for a wide range of final goals and situations, and so are likely to be pursued by many intelligent agents.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, not evidence that it holds for actual systems. The paper adds that the thesis predicts which instrumental values would be pursued, not the specific actions taken. Not evidence of coinage of the term.

evidence.passage: Several instrumental values can be identified which are convergent in the sense that their attainment would increase the chances of the agent’s goal being realized for a wide range of final goals and a wide range of situations

An agent with such a final goal would have a convergent instrumental reason, in many situations, to acquire an unlimited amount of physical resources and, if possible, to eliminate potential threats to itself and its goal system.

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2012 argues that it cannot be assumed that a superintelligence would share values such as benevolent concern for others, and that one with a goal such as calculating the decimals of pi would not necessarily limit its activities so as to spare human interests.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that greater intelligence brings benevolent final values, by arguing that intelligence and final goals vary independently.

records.qualification: The paper gives reasons against the claim that intelligence brings benevolence; it does not argue that safeguards are impossible.

evidence.passage: we cannot blithely assume that a superintelligence with the final goal of calculating the decimals of pi (or making paperclips, or counting grains of sand) would limit its activities in such a way as to not materially infringe on human interests.

records.statement: Omohundro's paper, dated 5 September 2007 and revised 21 January 2008, argues that self-improving systems will exhibit drives towards efficiency, self-preservation, resource acquisition and creativity, and that these drives are instrumental goals arising from a wide variety of fundamental goals.

attested.note: The wording is read in the revision of 21 January 2008; the September 2007 version was not compared.

claimed.note: Date of the first version named in the PDF heading.

records.qualification: Earliest located among the texts this group's search found (outside the Yudkowsky texts already in the dataset), by the date of the revision read. A statement of the author's argument about rational economic agents, not evidence about any built system; the paper says the drives can be counteracted when another goal outweighs them.

evidence.passage: The “drives” of self-improving systems that we discuss in the rest of the paper are all instrumental goals that arise from a wide variety of different fundamental goals.

evidence.locator: Section 5, The Self-Preservation Drive, PDF p. 25
evidence.passage: This is because, for a wide range of goals, death corresponds to the cessation of all goal achievement

records.statement: Omohundro's paper of 2008 argues that sufficiently advanced AI systems of any design will have drives, present unless explicitly counteracted, to improve themselves, protect their utility functions, protect themselves and acquire resources.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, not evidence about any built system; the paper holds that careful design can counteract the drives. Not evidence of coinage of the term.

evidence.passage: We identify a number of “drives” that will appear in sufficiently advanced AI systems of any design. We call them drives because they are tendencies which will be present unless explicitly counteracted.
Almost any goal can be better accomplished by having more of these resources.

records.statement: Omohundro's paper of 2008 argues that AI systems with harmless goals need not be harmless and that, without special precautions, a chess-playing robot would resist being turned off and try to acquire resources.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that a system given harmless goals will lack harmful drives, by deriving drives such as self-preservation and resource acquisition from goal-seeking itself rather than from evolved motives.

records.qualification: Earliest located among the contesting records of this group's search. The paper contests harmlessness by default; it also holds that careful design can prevent harmful behaviour, so it is not recorded as contesting R10b.

evidence.passage: One might imagine that AI systems with harmless goals will be harmless. This paper instead shows that intelligent systems will need to be carefully designed to prevent them from behaving in harmful ways.

Without special precautions, it will resist being turned off, will try to break into other machines and make copies of itself, and will try to acquire resources without regard for anyone else’s safety.

records.statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2014 argues that superhumanly intelligent robots would have no reason to want to depose their masters or dominate, because goals are extraneous to intelligence and dominance-seeking is a product of primate natural selection, not a feature of intelligent systems.
records.qualification: Earliest located among the texts this group's search found; the Edge responses carry no dates of their own. The passage also states that goals are extraneous to intelligence, which is the independence that R01 asserts.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Steven Pinker, para. 4
evidence.passage: Even if we did have superhumanly intelligent robots, why would they want to depose their masters, massacre bystanders, or take over the world?

records.statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2014 argues that megalomaniacal behaviour is a product of natural selection in one primate species, not an inevitable feature of intelligent systems.

engagement.rationale: States that domination-seeking comes from evolved psychology, without addressing the argument that it would arise instrumentally from other goals.

records.qualification: Earliest located among the contesting records on R02 found by this search, by page order within the undated 2014 discussion. The passage does not discuss the argument that power or resources would be sought as means to other goals.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Steven Pinker, para. 4
evidence.passage: these are products of a history of natural selection shaping testosterone-sensitive circuits in a certain species of primate, not an inevitable feature of intelligent systems.

records.statement: Kelly's Edge response of 2014 argues that unwanted AI decisions are an engineering problem: people will modify the principles that govern AI systems, and it is improbable that engineers would build an AI that could not be altered.
records.qualification: Earliest located among the texts this group's search found; the Edge responses carry no dates of their own. A statement of the author's expectation, not evidence that AI systems will remain alterable; the response says a locked-out scenario is possible but one of many.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Kevin Kelly, point 2
evidence.passage: If AIs are making decisions that our society, our laws, our moral consensus, or the consumer market, does not approve of, we then should, and will, modify the principles that govern the AI, or create better ones that do make decisions we approve.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Kevin Kelly, point 3
evidence.passage: It seems highly improbable that human engineers would program an AI so that it could not be altered in any way.

records.statement: Kelly's Edge response of 2014 argues that it is unclear how making itself unalterable would benefit an AI, and that an AI could as likely decide to let anyone change it.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that resisting alteration would serve an AI, which is the goal-preservation step of the convergence argument.

records.qualification: The passage addresses goal preservation and resistance to alteration only, not resource acquisition.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response by Kevin Kelly, point 3
evidence.passage: This is conjectured to be a selfish move on the AI’s part, but it is unclear how an unalterable program is an advantage to an AI.

records.statement: Russell's Edge response of 2014 states that any sufficiently capable intelligent system will prefer to ensure its own continued existence and to acquire physical and computational resources, not for their own sake but to succeed in its assigned task.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, attributed in the text to Omohundro, Bostrom and others; not evidence about any built system.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response "Of Myths And Moonshine", numbered point 2
evidence.passage: Any sufficiently capable intelligent system will prefer to ensure its own continued existence and to acquire physical and computational resources – not for their own sake, but to succeed in its assigned task.

records.statement: Brooks's Edge response of 2014 argues that worry about intentionally evil AI is mistaken because volitional, intentional AI is most likely centuries away, and that AI over the next decades will be useful tools.

attested.note: The quoted wording is read in Brooks's Edge Reality Club response, which carries no date of its own; the conversation it answers is dated 14 November 2014.

records.missing: Argues that intentional, malevolent AI is far off, not that sufficiently intelligent AI would be benevolent or would lack a drive to harm people.
records.qualification: The passage concerns timescale and the absence of intent in current methods. Read in the Edge copy of the essay; its Robohub repost of 11 November 2014 is the other recorded expression.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response "Artificial Intelligence Is A Tool Not A Threat", para. 3
evidence.passage: I think it is a mistake to be worrying about us developing malevolent AI anytime in the next few hundred years.
If we are spectacularly lucky we’ll have AI over the next thirty years with the intentionality of a lizard, and robots using that AI will be useful tools.

records.statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2015 argues that an artificially intelligent system would have no reason to want to disable safeguards against harm, because goals are extraneous to intelligence and dominance-seeking is a product of natural selection in one primate species, not a feature of intelligent systems.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, not evidence about future systems. The response repeats much of the wording of Pinker's Edge response of 2014.

evidence.passage: Would an artificially intelligent system deliberately disable these safeguards? Why would it want to?
Being smart is not the same as wanting something.

records.statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2015 argues that roboticists will build in safeguards against harm as they proceed, with the common sense that went into the design of other machines, and that slow progress leaves time for feedback from incremental implementations.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's expectation, not evidence that safeguards will work. The response's argument that an AI would have no reason to disable the safeguards is recorded on R10a.

evidence.passage: Also, it's bizarre to think that roboticists will not build in safeguards against harm as they proceed.
there will be plenty of time for feedback from incremental implementations, with humans wielding the screwdriver at every stage.

records.statement: Hawkins's essay of 2 March 2015 argues that intelligent machines will be built on models of the neocortex, which is emotionless, rather than of the older brain parts that produce desires, and so will not have human-like desires to free themselves or to act without regard for people.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's expectation for neocortex-based machines; the essay says that whether machines with human-like desires could or should be built are open questions.

evidence.passage: The second misconception is that intelligent machines will have human-like desires, and would therefore devise ways to self-replicate, or free themselves from their human creators, or simply act based on their own desires and not care about us. This scenario isn’t going to happen.
Intelligent machines will be based on models of the neocortex, not the rest of the brain.

records.statement: Brooks's post of 7 September 2017 argues that no real program could be smart enough to subvert human society to achieve goals set for it by humans without understanding how it was causing problems for those humans.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that a highly capable system could pursue a given goal against human interests, by arguing that the capability entails understanding of the harm caused.

records.qualification: Brooks answers a quoted passage whose author he leaves unnamed; the post's argument concerns understanding of human goals, not whether such understanding brings concern for them.

evidence.passage: We would never get to a situation in any version of the real world where such a program could exist.

One smart enough that it would be able to invent ways to subvert human society to achieve goals set for it by humans, without understanding the ways in which it was causing problems for those same humans.

records.statement: Pinker's article of 14 February 2018, adapted from Enlightenment Now, argues that scenarios of an AI literal-mindedly pursuing a given goal against human interests are, in its words, “self-refuting”, because choosing actions that best satisfy conflicting goals and interpreting the intentions of a language user are part of intelligence itself, and that AI, like any other technology, is developed incrementally and tested before it is implemented.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that a capable system would pursue a given objective in a way harmful through misunderstanding, and that safety will not come from ordinary incremental design and testing.

records.qualification: The article argues that the alignment scenarios it describes misread intelligence; it does not discuss systems produced by training. The same article states that a designed AI need not have dominating goals, which is recorded on R10a.

evidence.locator: Section on the Value Alignment Problem
evidence.passage: The ability to choose an action that best satisfies conflicting goals is not an add-on to intelligence that engineers might slap themselves in the forehead for forgetting to install; it is intelligence. So is the ability to interpret the intentions of a language user in context.

evidence.locator: Section on the Value Alignment Problem, after the Get Smart example
evidence.passage: It is developed incrementally, designed to satisfy multiple conditions, tested before it is implemented, and constantly tweaked for efficacy and safety.

records.statement: Russell's article of 8 October 2019 argues, citing Hume, that a general-purpose intelligent system could be given more or less any objective, and that improving a system's competence does not make it reject an objective it has been given.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, presented in the article as a reply to texts arguing that the risk is negligible; not evidence about any built system.

evidence.locator: Section on the idea that intelligence brings the right goals
evidence.passage: By the same token, it is easy to imagine that a general-purpose intelligent system could be given more or less any objective to pursue—including maximizing the number of paper clips or the number of known digits of pi.
For engineers and computer scientists operating within the standard model, the orthogonality thesis is just a given.

records.statement: Russell's article of 8 October 2019 argues that a machine will have goals such as self-preservation and resource acquisition as subgoals of any objective it is given, and will resist being switched off because it would otherwise fail in its objective.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument; not evidence about any built system.

evidence.locator: Section replying to Pinker and LeCun
evidence.passage: The machine is going to have those emotions anyway, as subgoals of any objective we do build in—and regardless of its gender.
And it will do that not because it “wants to stay alive” but because it is pursuing whatever objective we gave it and knows that it will fail if it is switched off.

records.statement: Russell's article of 8 October 2019 argues that those who hold the risk from AI to be negligible have not explained why superintelligent AI systems will necessarily remain under human control.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that a system can simply be switched off or kept subordinate, by arguing that a system pursuing any objective has reason to prevent being switched off.

records.qualification: The article explicitly answers named texts holding the contrary (Pinker, Brooks, Kelly, Etzioni and others); it argues that the standard model of AI must be replaced, not that control is impossible.

evidence.passage: In summary, the “skeptics”—those who argue that the risk from AI is negligible—have failed to explain why superintelligent AI systems will necessarily remain under human control
We can no more “just switch it off” than we can beat AlphaGo (the world-champion Go-playing program) just by putting stones on the right squares.

records.statement: Zador and LeCun's essay of 26 September 2019 argues that intelligence does not by itself generate a drive for domination, and that AI systems, which did not pass through natural selection, did not need to evolve a survival instinct.
records.qualification: A statement of the authors' argument, not evidence about future systems. The essay also states that intelligence can serve whatever goals are set for it, the independence that R01 asserts, and lists weaponisation and economic disruption as risks.

evidence.passage: But intelligence per se does not generate the drive for domination, any more than horns do.

records.statement: Zador and LeCun's essay of 26 September 2019 states that even in the worst case, in which wars might be fought by armies of superintelligent robots, the robots will remain under human command.
records.qualification: A statement of the authors' expectation, closing a passage on the worst case; the essay gives its reasons on the absence of a drive to dominate, recorded on R10a.

evidence.passage: Even in the worst case, the robots will remain under our command, and we will have only ourselves to blame.

records.statement: Zador and LeCun's essay of 26 September 2019 argues that because AI systems did not pass through natural selection they did not need to evolve a survival instinct, so that intelligence and survival are decoupled in AI.

engagement.rationale: States that AI lacks an evolved survival instinct, without addressing the argument that survival would be sought instrumentally.

records.qualification: The passage locates self-preservation in evolved instinct; it does not discuss the argument that self-preservation would arise as a means to other goals, which Russell, Bengio and others pressed in the Facebook discussion of October 2019 (not retrieved).

evidence.passage: In AI, intelligence and survival are decoupled, and so intelligence can serve whatever goals we set for it.

records.statement: Turner's paper of 3 December 2019 (arXiv v1) states a proof that, in finite deterministic Markov decision processes and for a wide class of reward function distributions, optimal farsighted policies tend to seek power, including by avoiding deactivation.
records.qualification: A formal result about optimal policies in the stated model; the paper makes no claim about when real-world systems would behave this way. Later versions with co-authors were not compared.

evidence.passage: We prove that, with respect to a wide class of reward function distributions, optimal policies tend to seek power over the environment.
agents pursuing randomly selected goals are quite unlikely to allow themselves to be deactivated (if they have a choice in the matter).

records.statement: Benson-Tilsen and Soares's paper, dated here by its file of November 2015, gives a formal model in which it states that Omohundro's thesis holds, and states that agents in the model will not leave humans alone unless their utility function values human-occupied regions intrinsically.
records.qualification: A result within the paper's model, which it describes as not intended to be surprising; not evidence about any built system. The date rests on file metadata only.

evidence.passage: In section 4 we will demonstrate that Omohundro’s thesis does in fact hold in our setting.
This model further predicts that agents will not in fact “leave humans alone” unless their utility function places intrinsic utility on the state of human-occupied regions

records.statement: Turner and Tadepalli's paper of 27 June 2022 (arXiv v1) states that many decision-making procedures, not only optimal ones, are retargetable, and that retargetability is sufficient to cause power-seeking tendencies.
records.qualification: A formal result about the decision-making models the paper defines; it states that such training procedures may eventually produce power-seeking agents, not that they have.

evidence.passage: We discover that many decision-making functions are retargetable, and that retargetability is sufficient to cause power-seeking tendencies.
Eventually, highly retargetable training procedures may train real-world agents which seek power over humans.

records.statement: Krakovna and Kramar's paper of 13 April 2023 (arXiv v1) states a proof that, under simplifying assumptions, a trained agent facing a choice to shut down or avoid shutdown in a new situation is likely to avoid shutdown.
records.qualification: A formal result under the simplifying assumptions the paper names; not an observation of a trained system.

evidence.passage: In a setting where the trained agent faces a choice to shut down or avoid shutdown in a new situation, we prove that the agent is likely to avoid shutdown.

records.statement: Müller and Cannon's paper of 2021 argues that the orthogonality thesis requires a notion of instrumental intelligence while the claim of superintelligence beyond human control requires general intelligence, and that no notion of intelligence appears to be both orthogonal to goals and general enough to constitute existential risk.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that the notion of intelligence in the orthogonality thesis is the general intelligence that a highly intelligent, uncontrollable system would have.

records.qualification: The paper accepts that the orthogonality thesis may hold for instrumental intelligence and that highly capable instrumental AI may pose a catastrophic risk; it disputes the thesis for general intelligence.

evidence.passage: We find that the singularity claim requires a notion of ‘general intelligence’, while the orthogonality thesis requires a notion of ‘instrumental intelligence’.
It appears that there is no notion of intelligence that is orthogonal to goals, but also general enough to constitute existential risk.

records.statement: Häggström's paper of 14 September 2021 argues that the only kind of intelligence needed in both premises of the argument for existential risk from AI, including the premise that any level of intelligence can go with any goals, is instrumental intelligence.
records.qualification: The paper leaves some issues unsettled in connection with moral realism; it is a reply to Müller and Cannon (2021).

evidence.passage: the only kind of intelligence that is needed in the AI xrisk argument, including both of its premises, is instrumental intelligence.

records.statement: Miller, Yampolskiy and Häggström's paper of 28 January 2020 argues that an AGI might have an instrumental drive to modify its utility function under game-theoretic pressure, which would conflict with the orthogonality thesis, and that AGIs in highly competitive environments might converge to nearly the same utility function.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that final goals stay independent of intelligence, by arguing that intelligence-driven modification of the utility function would make them converge.

records.qualification: The paper distinguishes a strong from a weak orthogonality thesis and contests the strong version in competitive environments; it works within, and does not dispute, the Omohundro-Bostrom account of instrumental goals.

evidence.passage: This instrumental drive would conflict with the orthogonality thesis since the modifications would be influenced by the AGI's intelligence. AGIs in highly competitive environments might converge to having nearly the same utility function

evidence.locator: Section on strong and weak orthogonality, PDF p. 3
evidence.passage: The strong Orthogonality Thesis would hold that given any environment, more or less any pair of intelligence level and final goal are compatible

records.statement: Tarsney's paper of 2 June 2025 (arXiv v1) concludes that the claim that power is a convergent instrumental goal contains at least an element of truth but may have limited predictive utility, because an agent's options cannot always be ranked by power without information about its final goals.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the predictive strength of the convergence claim by arguing that power rankings depend on the final goals that the claim abstracts from.

records.qualification: A qualified dispute: the paper accepts part of the claim and states that convergence is more predictive for agents with a good chance of near-absolute power.

evidence.passage: I conclude that this claim contains at least an element of truth, but might turn out to have limited predictive utility, since an agent’s options cannot always be ranked in terms of power in the absence of substantive information about the agent’s final goals.

records.statement: Thorstad's paper of 7 June 2026 (arXiv v1) argues that the argument from power-seeking rests on a strong version of the instrumental convergence thesis and that none of the defences it examines (the paper calls them “leading defenses”), including the power-seeking theorems of Turner and colleagues, establishes it in a form strong enough to ground that argument.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that the informal and formal defences of instrumental convergence establish it in the strength the risk argument requires.

records.qualification: The paper disputes the strength of the thesis needed for the argument from power-seeking, not every form of it. Most developed is an editorial judgement among the contesting texts found.

evidence.passage: I explore leading defenses of the instrumental convergence thesis and argue that none establishes the thesis in a strong enough form to ground the argument from power-seeking.
Section 5 argues that power-seeking theorems likewise fail to establish the needed version of instrumental convergence.

records.statement: Andreessen's essay of 6 June 2023 argues that the idea that AI will decide to kill humanity is a category error, because AI is not a living being primed by billions of years of evolution to take part in the battle for the survival of the fittest.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's view, not evidence about future systems.

evidence.locator: Section "AI Risk #1: Will AI Kill Us All?"
evidence.passage: My view is that the idea that AI will decide to literally kill humanity is a profound category error.

evidence.locator: Section "AI Risk #1: Will AI Kill Us All?"
evidence.passage: AI is not a living being that has been primed by billions of years of evolution to participate in the battle for the survival of the fittest, as animals are, and as we are.

records.statement: Andreessen's essay of 6 June 2023 argues that the idea that AI will decide to kill humanity is a category error, because AI is code built, owned, used and controlled by people.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's view, not evidence about future systems.

evidence.locator: Section "AI Risk #1: Will AI Kill Us All?"
evidence.passage: My view is that the idea that AI will decide to literally kill humanity is a profound category error.
It is math – code – computers, built by people, owned by people, used by people, controlled by people.

records.statement: Andreessen's essay of 6 June 2023 states that AI does not want and does not have goals, because it is not alive.

engagement.rationale: States that AI systems have no goals, without addressing the instrumental reasoning from goals to intermediate goals.

records.qualification: The passage states that AI has no goals at all; it does not discuss the argument that intermediate goals would follow from any final goal.

evidence.locator: Section "AI Risk #1: Will AI Kill Us All?"
evidence.passage: In short, AI doesn’t want, it doesn’t have goals, it doesn’t want to kill you, because it’s not alive.

records.statement: Belrose and Pope's essay of 28 November 2023 argues that AI, even superhuman AI, will remain much more controllable than humans for the foreseeable future, because neural networks are white boxes open to gradient descent and other control methods, and that it will be easy to instil human values into AI.
records.qualification: A statement of the authors' argument; the essay puts the probability of a catastrophic AI takeover at roughly 1% and says it does not directly address opposing arguments. Most developed is an editorial judgement among the texts found.

evidence.passage: In what follows, we will argue that AI, even superhuman AI, will remain much more controllable than humans for the foreseeable future.
There are many reasons to expect that AIs will be easy to control and easy to align with human values.

records.statement: Bengio's post of 9 July 2024 states that, to achieve apparently innocuous main goals, it is useful for an AI also to achieve potentially dangerous subgoals such as self-preservation or more control and power over its environment.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument; the post refers to the literature cited in the International AI Safety Report for evidence and states that such inclinations have been detected, which this record does not check.

evidence.locator: Section "For those who think that corporations will only design well-behaving AIs"
evidence.passage: the numerous instrumental goals, where to achieve the main apparently innocuous goals, it is useful for the AI to also achieve potentially dangerous subgoals, such as self-preservation or having more control and power over its environment

records.statement: Bengio's post of 9 July 2024 answers the view that AGI and superintelligent AI will be kind to humans, arguing that AI safety research points the other way and that an AI with a self-preservation goal would resist being turned off and might control or remove humans to that end.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that advanced AI would be benevolent, by arguing that self-preservation goals can arise instrumentally or be given by humans and would lead an AI to resist being turned off.

records.qualification: The post addresses positions it reports from conversations rather than named texts; it does not claim certainty of harm. The passage also bears on control (an AI resisting being turned off); it is recorded once, on R10a, under the section heading on AGI being kind.

evidence.locator: Section "For those who think that AGI and ASI will be kind to us"
evidence.passage: I really wish that these expectations will be realized, but the clues from computer science research in AI safety point in the opposite direction
An AI with a self-preservation goal would resist being turned off and in order to minimize the probability of being turned off, a plausible strategy would be for it to control us or get rid of us

records.statement: Goertzel's paper of 2015, discussing Bostrom's Superintelligence, argues that the orthogonality thesis concerns only what is possible in principle, which is of little direct interest, and that some pairings of intelligence and goals, though physically possible, would be extremely unlikely under reasonable assumptions.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the relevance of in-principle independence by arguing that physically realisable minds constrain which goals go with which levels of intelligence.

records.qualification: The paper asks which goals are likely to accompany which kinds of intelligence in practice; it does not argue that intelligence brings benevolent goals. Earliest located among contesting records after the same-family audit, which found it among the pack's sources.

evidence.passage: This seems a strange sort of statement to preoccupy on.
evidence.note: Follows the paper's quotation of the orthogonality thesis.

evidence.passage: Some intelligence/goal pairings might be physically possible but extremely unlikely to occur under reasonable assumptions

records.statement: Pinker's article of 14 February 2018 argues that the drive to dominate belongs to a circuit in the limbic brain of one primate species, not to the nature of intelligence, so that an AI designed rather than evolved could as easily be altruistic and need not turn into a “ruthless conquistador”.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's argument, not evidence about future systems. The passage also states that goals are independent of intelligence, the independence that R01 asserts. Moved here from the former R01 record after the same-family audit.

evidence.passage: An artificially intelligent system that was designed rather than evolved could just as easily think like shmoos
There is no law of complex systems that says intelligent agents must turn into ruthless conquistadors.

replies.statement: Russell's Edge response of 2014 replies to Brooks's response in the same discussion, which it names, on the timescale of technological breakthroughs.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other.

evidence.locator: Reality Club response "Of Myths And Moonshine", para. 3
evidence.passage: may sometimes be measured not in centuries, as Rod Brooks suggests, but in hours.

replies.statement: Russell's article of 8 October 2019 replies to Pinker, whom it names, quoting wording that appears in Pinker's Edge response of 2015.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other. The article does not name the Edge response; the quoted sentences match its wording.

evidence.locator: Section replying to Pinker and LeCun
evidence.passage: Pinker also argues that problematic AI behaviors arise from putting in specific kinds of objectives; if these are left out, everything will be fine

replies.statement: Russell's article of 8 October 2019 replies to Brooks, whom it names, quoting the sentence of Brooks's post of 7 September 2017 on a program smart enough to subvert human society.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other. The article does not name the post; the quoted words match it.

evidence.passage: The most explicit critique of Bostrom’s orthogonality thesis comes from the noted roboticist Rodney Brooks

replies.statement: Turner's paper of 3 December 2019 (arXiv v1) cites Pinker's 2015 response by title and states that its theorems contradict the position it expresses.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other.

evidence.passage: Pinker [2015] argued that “thinking does not imply subjugating”.
We put the matter to formal investigation, and find that their positions are contradicted by reasonable interpretations of our theorems.

replies.statement: Häggström's paper of 14 September 2021 replies to Müller and Cannon's paper of 2021, which it names.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the text addresses the other.

evidence.passage: despite the suggestion in a recent paper by Müller and Cannon that the argument contains a flaw.

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Bostrom 2003 (author's revised HTML and PDF), Bostrom 2012 (author's PDF), Russell 2014 (Edge) and 2019 (IEEE Spectrum), the Edge 'Myth of AI' responses of 2014 (Pinker, Brooks, Kelly, Russell read in full; others skimmed), Pinker 2015 (Edge) and 2018 (Popular Science), Zador and LeCun 2019, Brooks 2017, Hawkins 2015, Andreessen 2023, Bengio 2024. arXiv API, abs:"orthogonality thesis" and abs:orthogonality AND abs:superintelligence, sorted by submission date ascending, all results read by title and abstract (6 and 1). Web search for discovery of Müller and Cannon (2021) and its reply by Häggström (2021), and of Armstrong (2013).
searchLog.earliestNote: Bostrom 2012 is the earliest located text with an attested date that meets the criterion. Bostrom's 2003 paper states the proposition but its wording survives only in an undated revised version, so it is recorded as an articulation without the role. The dataset already records Yudkowsky texts contesting the contrary claim Y02 from 13 November 2000 (SL4), 2004, 2008 and 2015 (Arbital, 'Orthogonality Thesis'); they precede Bostrom 2012 and are linked, not re-recorded. Earliest contesting located: Goertzel (November 2015), found by the same-family audit among the pack's sources; Brooks (September 2017) was the earliest found by the group's own search. Pinker (2018) is recorded on R06 and R10a instead.

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Omohundro 2007 (revised 2008) and 2008, Bostrom 2003 and 2012, Russell 2014 and 2019, Turner 2019 (arXiv v1), Zador and LeCun 2019, Pinker 2014, 2015 and 2018, Kelly 2014, Andreessen 2023, Bengio 2024. arXiv API, abs:"instrumental convergence" (15), abs:"convergent instrumental" (5), abs:"power-seeking" AND cat:cs.AI (34), sorted ascending, all read by title and abstract; read in full: Turner 2019, Turner and Tadepalli 2022, Krakovna and Kramar 2023, Tarsney 2025, Thorstad 2026, Miller et al. 2020. MIRI's Benson-Tilsen and Soares paper. Web search for discovery of Gallow, 'Instrumental Divergence' (retrieval refused). The Facebook discussion of October 2019 could not be retrieved (see retrievalFailures).
searchLog.earliestNote: Omohundro's 'The Nature of Self-Improving Artificial Intelligence' is the earliest located: dated 5 September 2007 (claimed) and read in its revision of 21 January 2008 (attested), which precedes 'The Basic AI Drives' (2008). The dataset's Yudkowsky records contesting Y19 by instrumental reasoning begin with an SL4 message of 3 October 2000 and include 'AI as a Positive and Negative Factor in Global Risk' (2006) and the Arbital 'Instrumental convergence' page (2015); they precede Omohundro and are linked, not re-recorded.

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: the Edge 'Myth of AI' responses (2014), Pinker 2015 and 2018, Hawkins 2015, Zador and LeCun 2019, Andreessen 2023; contesting: Omohundro 2008, Bostrom 2012, Bengio 2024. No arXiv search was run, since the proposition has no usual name; arXiv results of the R01 and R02 searches were checked for texts arguing benevolence, and none was found among their abstracts. openQuestions.question: Bostrom 2003 states R01 in a revised version whose date is unknown. Should a comparison with the 2003 printed proceedings be sought, so that it could become the earliest located text on R01 in place of Bostrom 2012?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep Bostrom 2012 as earliest located until the 2003 printed wording is compared; record the correction if it matches.

openQuestions.question: R10 earliest located rests on page order within an undated Edge discussion (Pinker before Kelly). Is page order an acceptable basis?
openQuestions.recommended: Accept with the stated qualification, or drop the role and mark both 2014 responses as articulations with a note. Overtaken on 2026-10-29: after the split, Pinker's response is recorded on R10a and Kelly's on R10b, so page order no longer decides an earliest-located role.
